d.title: output_key is how one agent hands work to the next
d.caption: **There is no pipe between agents — there is state, and `output_key` is the write.** When the agent produces its final text ADK attaches it to the final event as a state delta, exactly like any other state change (lesson 1.4), and the session service applies it on append. The next agent's instruction then reads it back by name through templating. **That pair is the entire data-flow mechanism of a sequential pipeline:** one agent writes `{draft}`, the next one's instruction interpolates it. With an `output_schema` the parsed dict is written instead of the raw string.

nodes.label: The next agent's instruction reads it
With output_schema, a dict is written

d.title: What a schema costs, and what changed in 2.x
d.caption: **The version matters here more than the feature does.** In ADK 1.x setting `output_schema` disabled tools and transfer, which is the advice still repeated in most writing about this; in 2.x the framework exposes tools during the thought loop and enforces structure only on the final output, so the two compose. **And note what lands in state: a plain dict** — not the Pydantic instance and not the JSON string — so a downstream agent reading `{summary}` gets data rather than an object with methods.

d.title: Three instruction fields, in the order they reach the model
d.caption: **Read the order, because it is the whole design.** The global instruction comes first and is prepended for every descendant too, so a refusal rule written once at the root cannot be forgotten in a specialist three levels down. **The static instruction is the cacheable half:** anything in `instruction` is re-rendered every call because state may have changed, so it can never be cached — moving two thousand tokens of style guide into `static_instruction` changes nothing about behaviour and a great deal about cost (lesson 5.6). ADK then appends its own transfer guidance when the agent has sub-agents.

items.sub: this agent; state interpolated fresh each call

items.label: ADK's own framing
items.sub: the agent's name, and transfer guidance if it has children

d.title: A dynamic instruction is context, not enforcement
d.caption: **The temptation is to compute permissions here — *if the user is not an admin, tell the model not to use the delete tool* — and a model may simply ignore it.** An instruction is a request, and the whole lesson of this module is that a request is not a control. Access control belongs in a `before_tool_callback` that refuses the call, or in not giving that agent the tool at all. **Use the callable form for what templating cannot express:** a lookup, the time of day, a computed list — and note that `ReadonlyContext` is readonly by design, so nothing here can mutate state.

nodes.sub: refuse the call, or omit the tool

d.title: Three agents, three events, three state keys
d.caption: **The hand-off is confirmed by the last line: the critic's assembled instruction contained the writer's text**, which is `output_key` plus templating doing the work with no wiring of your own. The point of the measurement is the row above it: **every child reports `is_final_response()` as true**, so a front end that renders every final event shows all three drafts — the filtering problem from lesson 1.5, arriving as soon as you compose agents. **And a sequential pipeline costs zero routing calls**, where an LLM coordinator over the same three agents costs at least three and can mis-route.

d.title: Four things a custom agent yields, and the one that does not work
d.caption: **`BaseAgent` asks for one method, and everything the framework needs happens through what you yield.** An event needs only an invocation id and an author — content is optional, so an event can exist purely to carry a state delta or an escalation. **The last row is the mistake everyone makes once:** assigning to `ctx.session.state` looks like it works and does not persist, because the delta on the event is what the session service applies. And the dividing line for reaching for this at all: a custom agent is for control *flow*; work that calls an API belongs in a tool, where it is testable alone and visible to the model.

d.title: Two flags turn a specialist into a terminal node
d.caption: **Set both and the conversation stays where it arrived for the rest of the invocation**, which is usually what a checkout or an authentication flow wants — wandering off mid-transaction is the failure mode there. Leave both at their defaults on every agent and you get conversations that ping-pong, which is the argument for shaping the tree deliberately rather than making every agent a sibling of every other. **And the trap worth repeating: a coordinator with tools of its own is not a coordinator** — its model must choose between answering and delegating every turn, and models prefer answering.

d.title: The coordinator pattern, with its failure mode named
d.caption: **The pattern works when a user can only be in one domain at a time, and fails on the question that straddles two** — a refund for an outage belongs to billing and to tech, and whichever specialist receives it answers half of it. **The routing information is the `description` field, not the instruction**, so disjoint descriptions written in the user's vocabulary are the actual fix for mis-routing; and allowing transfer back to the parent is what lets a specialist return a question it cannot own. Evaluate the routing with a trajectory evalset rather than by trying prompts.

state: domains a user is in one of at a time
disjoint descriptions, in the user's words
allow transfer back; test with an evalset

d.title: Eight tools become one declaration
d.caption: **Accuracy falls as the declaration list grows, and the fall is steep somewhere past about ten tools** — the exact number depends on the model and on how distinct the tools are. So a tool list that has grown past ten is a grouping signal rather than a prompt-tuning problem: wrap the related tools in an agent and expose it with `AgentTool`, and the caller sees one well-described capability. **The token saving is the same mechanism:** the sub-agent's eight declarations are only sent when the sub-agent actually runs, so the outer agent's every turn stops paying for them.
